# 1. Overview

This exercise applies spatial point pattern analysis methods to study the distribution of newly registered corporate entities in Singapore. Following the Data Analytics Lifecycle and based on the hands-on practices, the analysis covers data preparation, industry classification, geocoding, and geovisualisation.

⚠️ Note: Running all three industries (Food & Beverage, IT Services, Education) together caused very long rendering times on Netlify. To ensure smooth deployment, this report only keeps the **Food & Beverage** industry code for demonstration. The full analysis for IT Services and Education has been computed locally and results are available upon request.

## 2. **Installing and Launching the R Packages**



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
pacman::p_load(tidyverse, readr, lubridate,sf,tmap, rvest,httr, jsonlite, dplyr, purrr,spatstat,terra,spatstat.explore,stars,spatstat.geom,rlang)
```
:::





## 3. Data Import & Preparation

The following 3 datasets will be used in this exercise.

-   ACRA (Accounting and Corporate Regulatory Authority) Information on Corporate Entities datasets from data.gov.sg

-   postal code download by onemap

-   Master Plan 2019 Subzone Boundary (No Sea), a polygon feature data providing information of URA 2019 Master Plan Planning Subzone boundary data.

Import ACRA datasets from **data.gov.sg**.



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
acra_files <- list.files("data/aspatial/ACRA", 
                         pattern = "*.csv", 
                         full.names = TRUE)
```
:::

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
acra_raw <- map_dfr(acra_files, read_csv)
```
:::



Select relevant fields and filter entities registered between **1 Jan 2024 and 30 Jun 2025**.



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
acra_clean <- acra_raw %>%
  select(
    uen,
    entity_name,
    ssic_code = primary_ssic_code,
    ssic_desc = primary_ssic_description,
    postal = postal_code,
    reg_date = registration_incorporation_date
  ) %>%
  filter(reg_date >= "2024-01-01", reg_date <= "2025-06-30") %>%
  filter(!is.na(postal)) %>%
  distinct(uen, .keep_all = TRUE)   
   
glimpse(acra_clean)
```

## 4.3 Clark-Evan Test for Nearest Neighbour Analysis

The Clark-Evans test (Nearest Neighbour Analysis, NNA) is a spatial statistics method that calculates the average distance between each point and its closest neighbor to determine if a pattern of points is clustered, dispersed, or randomly distributed.\

We will perform the Clark-Evans test of aggregation for each selected industry by using `clarkevans.test()` of **spatstat.explore** package.

The general test hypotheses are:

-   **H0**: The distribution of business entities is randomly distributed (CSR – Complete Spatial Randomness).

-   **H1**: The distribution of business entities is not randomly distributed (i.e., significantly clustered or dispersed).

The 95% confidence interval will be used.

### **4.3.1 Perform the Clark-Evans test without CSR**

#### 4.3.1.1 Food & Beverage (SSIC 56)

For **Food & Beverage** industry, the hypotheses are:

-   **H0**: The distribution of Food & Beverage businesses is randomly distributed.

-   **H1**: The distribution of Food & Beverage businesses is not randomly distributed.



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
sub_fnb <- acra_sf_proj %>% filter(ssic_2d == "56")
coords_fnb <- st_coordinates(sub_fnb)
ppp_fnb <- spatstat.geom::ppp(x = coords_fnb[,1], y = coords_fnb[,2],window = sg_owin)

clarkevans.test(ppp_fnb,
                correction = "none",
                clregion = "sg_owin",
                alternative = c("clustered"))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

	Clark-Evans test
	No edge correction
	Z-test

data:  ppp_fnb
R = 0.34006, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: clustered (R < 1)
```


:::
:::



**Insights:**

-   Clark-Evans test gives **R = 0.36, p \< 0.001**, shows **significantly clustered**.

-   This means F&B outlets are not randomly distributed but significantly concentrated in certain locations.

#### 4.3.1.2 IT Services (SSIC 62)

For **IT Services** industry, the hypotheses are:

-   **H0**: The distribution of IT Services businesses is randomly distributed.

-   **H1**: The distribution of IT Services businesses is not randomly distributed.

**Insights:**

-   Clark-Evans test gives **R = 0.25, p \< 0.001**, indicating **strong clustering**.

-   The distribution is highly concentrated, suggesting strong spatial dependence.

#### 4.3.1.3 Education (SSIC 85)

For **Education** industry, the hypotheses are:

H0: The distribution of Education businesses is randomly distributed.

H1: The distribution of Education businesses is not randomly distributed.

**Insights:**

-   Clark-Evans test gives **R = 0.37, p \< 0.001**, also **significantly clustered**.

-   Education providers tend to be located in specific zones rather than evenly across Singapore.

### **4.3.2 Perform the Clark-Evans test with CSR**

In the code chunk below, the argument method = “MonteCarlo” is used. In this case, the p-value for the test is computed by comparing the observed value of R to the results obtained from nsim (i.e. 39, 99, 999) simulated realisations of Complete Spatial Randomness conditional on the observed number of points.



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ce_fnb <- readRDS("data/aspatial/kde_rds/CE_FNB.rds")
```
:::

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ce_fnb
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

	Clark-Evans test
	No edge correction
	Monte Carlo test based on 99 simulations of CSR with fixed n

data:  ppp_fnb
R = 0.3612, p-value = 0.01
alternative hypothesis: clustered (R < 1)
```


:::
:::



-   The significant R \< 1 indicates strong clustering. F&B businesses tend to group around popular dining districts and residential catchments, reflecting demand-driven location strategies.
-   The lowest R among the three industries, suggesting the strongest clustering. This likely reflects concentration in CBDs and business parks where digital and consultancy firms prefer proximity to clients and talent.
-   Also shows clear clustering, though slightly weaker than IT. This may align with population density, as educational services are concentrated in residential towns and central areas.

## **5. Kernel Density Estimation Method**

**Kernel Density Estimation (KDE)** is a valuable tool for visualising and analyzing first-order spatial point patterns. It is widely considered a method within **Exploratory Spatial Data Analysis (ESDA).** We will use Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) is applied to visualize the spatial intensity of newly registered businesses. It helps us **identify hotspots, highlight areas with high clustering**, and provides a clearer picture of the spatial distribution pattern beyond point maps.

### **5.1 Working with automatic bandwidth selection method**

Bandwidth selectors：

-   bw.diggle(): conservative (controls false positives); good general default.

-   bw.CvL(): Cressie–Read cross-validation; tends to optimize predictive fit.

-   bw.scott(): rule-of-thumb; reasonable for near-uniform patterns.

-   bw.ppl(): profile pseudo-likelihood; often a robust first choice.

-   Kernel: use gaussian (default); alternatives: "epanechnikov", "quartic", "disc".

-   Edge correction: set edge = TRUE (Jones, 1993; Diggle, 2010) to reduce boundary underestimation.

-   Coordinate system: run KDE in a metric projection (e.g., EPSG:3414) because it depends on distances.

-   Units: density.ppp() returns intensity per m²; multiply by 1e6 (10\^6) to report per km².



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Food & Beverage
kde_SG_fnb <- density(
  acra_56SG_ppp,
  sigma = bw.diggle(acra_56SG_ppp),
  edge = TRUE,
  kernel = "gaussian"
)
```
:::

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
kde_SG_fnb <- density(
  acra_56SG_ppp,
  sigma=bw.diggle,
  edge=TRUE,
  kernel="gaussian") 

plot(kde_SG_fnb)
```

### **5.4 Working with different kernel methods**

By default, the kernel method used in *density.ppp()* is *gaussian*. But there are three other options, namely: Epanechnikov, Quartic and Dics. The code chunk below will be used to compute three more kernel density estimations by using these three kernel function.

-   **Food & Beverage KDE (different kernels)**



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}

plot(density(ppp_fnb_km, sigma=0.4952614, edge=TRUE, kernel="gaussian"),
     main="F&B - Gaussian")
plot(density(ppp_fnb_km, sigma=0.4952614, edge=TRUE, kernel="epanechnikov"),
     main="F&B - Epanechnikov")
plot(density(ppp_fnb_km, sigma=0.4952614, edge=TRUE, kernel="quartic"),
     main="F&B - Quartic")
plot(density(ppp_fnb_km, sigma=0.4952614, edge=TRUE, kernel="disc"),
```

Across all three sectors, KDE reveals a stable **polycentric** pattern: the CBD–Orchard/River Valley spine, **Jurong East**, and **Tampines** persist as the highest-intensity hotspots. **IT Services** is the most tightly clustered, peaking in the Downtown Core and adjacent innovation corridors, reflecting proximity to clients and talent. **F&B** is more diffuse but concentrates along retail/nightlife belts (Orchard) and transit-anchored regional centres (Jurong East, Tampines). **Education** shows moderate clustering that aligns with dense residential towns and a central tutoring belt. Bandwidth checks (e.g., *bw.diggle* vs *bw.ppl*) alter smoothness, not hotspot locations—so peaks are **robust**. These first-order results anticipate

## **6 Fixed and Adaptive KDE**

### **6.1 Computing KDE by using fixed bandwidth**

Compute a KDE layer by your define.



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Fixed-bandwidth KDE: 600 m = 0.6 km
kde_fnb_fb <- density.ppp(ppp_fnb_km, sigma = 0.6, edge = TRUE, kernel = "gaussian")
plot(kde_fnb_fb, main = "KDE (Fixed 600 m) – F&B")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Take-Home_Exercise01_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-26-1.png){width=576}
:::
:::



New **F&B** entities cluster along the **CBD–Orchard–Chinatown** strip, extending east–west toward **Tampines** and **Jurong East**. Peripheral activity is sparse. The fixed bandwidth highlights a **broad core** shaped by commuter flows and tourism, while secondary intensity at regional hubs reflects mall-based demand and interchange footfall. The macro surface suggests F&B expansion remains **transit- and destination-oriented**, favouring large, mixed-use centres over dispersed neighbourhood sites.

New **IT** firms concentrate along the **CBD–Orchard–one-north** axis, reflecting proximity to Grade-A offices, venture services and universities. **Secondary intensity** appears at **Jurong East** and **Tampines**, consistent with regional business-hub functions and good MRT connectivity. North and far-west display sparse activity. The large, smooth kernel reveals a **strong core–periphery gradient** rather than scattered outposts, implying agglomeration benefits still dominate early-stage location choice. Compared with Education, IT shows a **tighter inner-core** and fewer peripheral pockets, consistent with knowledge-worker clustering and client proximity.

**Education**-related entities show **central-east hotspots** near dense residential estates and schools, plus signals around **Jurong East** and **Tampines**. The surface is **more diffuse** than IT, implying catchment-driven siting near learners rather than CBD client access. The fixed bandwidth emphasizes broad demand corridors connecting central estates to regional centres. Peripheral towns register **low but present** activity, suggesting incremental growth where population density and schools overlap.

### **6.2 Computing KDE by using adaptive bandwidth**

Fixed bandwidth method is very sensitive to highly skew distribution of spatial point patterns over geographical units for example urban versus rural. We can solve the problem by using adaptive bandwidth instead.



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
kde_fnb_ab <- adaptive.density(ppp_fnb_km, method="kernel")
plot(kde_fnb_fb, main = "kde_fnb_ab")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Take-Home_Exercise01_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-27-1.png){width=576}
:::
:::



Adaptive KDE sharpens **street-level cores** in the **CBD/Orchard/Chinatown** strip and reveals **compact neighbourhood centres** at **Jurong East** and **Tampines**. Smaller peaks align with MRT interchanges and mall clusters, indicating **transit-oriented footfall** as a strong predictor. Compared to fixed bandwidth, adaptive smoothing uncovers **micro-hotspots** that were previously blended into the urban core, useful for site selection and storefront competition mapping.

Education pockets appear as **small, localized clusters** embedded in residential towns, with compact peaks near **Tampines** and **Jurong East** and scattered central-east nodes. Adaptive smoothing shows a **fine-grained, catchment-based** structure: multiple modest centres rather than a single dominant core. This supports a **distributed service** model aligned with school density and family housing.

Let's take a look the difference:



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}

plot(kde_fnb_fb, main = "Fixed bandwidth")
plot(kde_fnb_ab, main = "Adaptive bandwidth")
```

## **7 Plotting cartographic quality KDE map**

```{.r .cell-code}
extract_kml_field <- function(html_text, field_name) {
  if (is.na(html_text) || html_text == "") return(NA_character_)
  
  page <- read_html(html_text)
  rows <- page %>% html_elements("tr")
  
  value <- rows %>%
    keep(~ html_text2(html_element(.x, "th")) == field_name) %>%
    html_element("td") %>%
    html_text2()
  
  if (length(value) == 0) NA_character_ else value
}

mpsz_sf <- mpsz_sf %>%
  mutate(
    REGION_N = map_chr(Description, extract_kml_field, "REGION_N"),
    PLN_AREA_N = map_chr(Description, extract_kml_field, "PLN_AREA_N"),
    SUBZONE_N = map_chr(Description, extract_kml_field, "SUBZONE_N"),
    SUBZONE_C = map_chr(Description, extract_kml_field, "SUBZONE_C")
  ) %>%
  select(-Name, -Description) %>%
  relocate(geometry, .after = last_col())

mpsz_sf <- mpsz_sf %>%
  filter(SUBZONE_N != "SOUTHERN GROUP",
         PLN_AREA_N != "WESTERN ISLANDS",
```

**F&B STKDE (Jan–Jun 2025) — key insights**

Across months, intensity concentrates in Orchard and parts of Tampines, with weaker, more fragmented activity in Jurong East and the Downtown Core. Orchard shows a persistent west–central hotspot that strengthens in Apr–Jun, suggesting steady retail-driven entry. Tampines exhibits a south-western focus in Jan–Feb, dips in Mar–Apr, then rebounds by Jun—consistent with phased openings around town-center corridors. Jurong East remains comparatively cool, with small pockets near transit nodes, while the Downtown Core stays low and stable, likely reflecting higher costs and corporate-office bias rather than F&B formation. Overall, spatial peaks are stable in place but vary in magnitude month-to-month, indicating cyclical demand rather than wholesale shifts in preferred locations.

How these findings can be used to support urban land use planning and management？

The maps and statistics reveal distinct formation logics by sector and location. F&B concentrates along pedestrian-rich retail corridors (Orchard, Tampines) and at transit interchanges, with month-to-month amplitude changes but stable geography. IT Services cluster tightly in innovation and Grade-A office precincts (one-north, CBD fringe). Education openings are broader, following residential catchments and access to schools and MRT. K/L functions exceeding CSR at short–medium ranges confirm clustering for F&B and IT; Education shows milder, short-range aggregation; the Downtown Core exhibits near-random patterns for F&B.

Transport and public realm. Because clusters align with MRT nodes, extend the “station halo” through shade, seating, lighting, and wayfinding to pull demand onto adjacent streets and reduce rent pressure on prime frontages. In Tampines and Orchard, support evening economy with footpath capacity, loading windows, and event-period crowd management aligned to the observed Apr–Jun lift.

Commercial space strategy. Time unit releases and tenders to sectoral cycles: pre-lease ahead of Q2 surges in Orchard; streamline fit-out in Q1–Q2 for Tampines. Curate Downtown Core edge locations (waterfronts, heritage lanes) for lifestyle anchors to diversify beyond office demand without over-concentrating F&B.

Sector-specific support. For IT, preserve affordable, flexible floorspace (co-working, labs) near one-north and CBD fringe; ensure top-tier digital infrastructure and last-mile links to universities. For Education, prioritize safe routes, ground-floor accessibility, and proximity to estates where diffuse but steady demand appears.

Targeting public-realm upgrades, flexible zoning, timed space releases, and sector-specific programs to these empirically observed patterns will yield low-regret, place-sensitive actions that grow vibrant, inclusive commercial districts while managing externalities.
